subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Troubles at home: religion, Mary Queen of Scots and rebellion
Troubles abroad: conflict with Spain and the Armada

questions.q: In which year did Elizabeth I establish her Religious Settlement?
questions.explain: The 1559 Religious Settlement comprised the Act of Supremacy and the Act of Uniformity.

questions.q: What title did Elizabeth I take as head of the Church of England?
options: Supreme Head of the Church
Supreme Governor of the Church
Defender of the Faith
Archbishop of Canterbury
questions.explain: She chose 'Supreme Governor' rather than 'Supreme Head' to reassure Catholics and those uneasy about a woman leading the Church.

questions.q: Who was Elizabeth's Secretary of State and closest adviser, later made Lord Burghley?
options: Francis Walsingham
William Cecil
Robert Dudley
Thomas Cromwell
questions.explain: William Cecil served Elizabeth as her most trusted adviser for most of her reign and was created Lord Burghley in 1571.

questions.q: Which of Elizabeth's ministers ran her spy network and uncovered Catholic plots?
options: William Cecil
Francis Walsingham
Robert Devereux
Francis Drake
questions.explain: Sir Francis Walsingham was Elizabeth's spymaster whose agents exposed plots such as the Babington Plot.

questions.q: In which year did the Spanish Armada sail against England?
questions.explain: Philip II launched the Armada in 1588, which was defeated in the English Channel and North Sea.

questions.q: Who was appointed by Philip II to command the Spanish Armada?
options: The Duke of Parma
The Duke of Medina Sidonia
The Duke of Alba
King Philip II himself
questions.explain: The Duke of Medina Sidonia led the Armada despite having little naval experience, after the original commander died.

questions.q: What was the name of the first purpose-built playhouse in London, opened by James Burbage in 1576?
options: The Globe
The Rose
The Theatre
The Swan
questions.explain: James Burbage built 'The Theatre' in Shoreditch in 1576, the first permanent playhouse in England.

questions.q: In which year did Mary Queen of Scots flee to England seeking Elizabeth's protection?
questions.explain: Mary Queen of Scots arrived in England in 1568 after being forced from the Scottish throne, becoming a focus for Catholic plots.

questions.q: Why did Elizabeth pursue a religious 'middle way' in her Settlement?
options: To convert all subjects to Catholicism
To create a compromise most people could accept and reduce religious conflict
To please the Pope in Rome
To abolish the Church of England
questions.explain: The Settlement blended Protestant doctrine with some traditional practices to unite as many subjects as possible and avoid unrest.

questions.q: Why did Elizabeth choose never to marry?
options: She was forbidden by law from marrying
To keep her independence and avoid handing power to a husband or foreign nation
Because no suitors ever proposed to her
Parliament banned her from marrying
questions.explain: Marriage risked giving control to a husband or entangling England with a foreign power, so Elizabeth used her single status as a diplomatic tool.

questions.q: Which of these best explains the main reasons for growing conflict between England and Spain?
options: A disagreement over trade tariffs alone
Religious differences, English piracy against Spanish treasure, and English support for Dutch rebels
A dispute over who should inherit the English throne
England's alliance with France against Spain
questions.explain: Protestant-Catholic rivalry, raids by 'sea dogs' like Drake, and English aid to Dutch rebels combined to push the two powers towards war.

questions.q: Why were the English fireships at Calais so effective against the Armada?
options: They sank most of the Spanish fleet
They forced the Spanish to cut their anchors and break their defensive crescent formation
They blocked the entire English Channel
They ferried Parma's army back to Spain
questions.explain: Fearing the burning ships, the Spanish panicked and scattered, losing the tight formation that had protected them.

questions.q: What was the main effect of the Pope's 1570 excommunication of Elizabeth (the bull Regnans in Excelsis)?
options: It forced Elizabeth to convert to Catholicism
It released English Catholics from loyalty to Elizabeth, increasing the threat of plots
It ended all Catholic worship in England
It recognised Elizabeth as Supreme Head of the Church
questions.explain: By declaring Elizabeth deposed, the bull encouraged Catholics to plot against her and made the government treat them with greater suspicion.

questions.q: Which combination best explains the increase in poverty in Elizabethan England?
options: Falling population and cheap food
Population growth, rising prices, enclosure and poor harvests
Government overspending on the navy
A sharp fall in the price of wool
questions.explain: A rising population, inflation, the enclosure of farmland and bad harvests together drove more people into poverty and vagrancy.

questions.q: Why did Puritans object to the Elizabethan theatre?
options: They thought tickets were too expensive
They believed plays encouraged sin and idleness and drew people away from church
They wanted to run the theatres themselves
They thought actors were paid too little
questions.explain: Puritans saw playhouses as immoral places that spread vice, disorder and disease and distracted people from religion.

questions.q: Why did the Earl of Essex's rebellion of 1601 fail?
options: The Spanish refused to send him support
Londoners and other nobles failed to back him and he was quickly arrested
Elizabeth immediately pardoned him
Parliament sided with him against the queen
questions.explain: Essex marched into London expecting popular support but received none, was swiftly captured and executed for treason.

questions.q: A Catholic gentleman is caught in 1586 exchanging coded letters in a scheme to assassinate Elizabeth and put Mary Queen of Scots on the throne. Which plot is this, and what did it lead to?
options: The Ridolfi Plot, which led to Norfolk's execution
The Throckmorton Plot, which led to Spain's expulsion
The Babington Plot, which led to Mary Queen of Scots' execution
The Northern Rebellion, which led to the fall of two earls
questions.explain: The Babington Plot of 1586, exposed by Walsingham, provided the evidence used to try and execute Mary in 1587.

questions.q: The Spanish plan required the Armada to meet the Duke of Parma's army in the Netherlands before invading England. Which problem most undermined this plan?
options: Parma's army was fully ready and waiting at the coast
Poor communication left Parma's army unready, with no deep-water port to embark from
The Armada arrived a full year too early
Parma refused to keep fighting the Dutch rebels
questions.explain: The Armada and Parma could not coordinate, and Parma lacked a safe deep-water port, so the invasion force could never link up.

questions.q: Under Elizabethan poor relief, a healthy man who refuses to work and roams the country begging would most likely be classed as which type of poor and treated how?
options: Deserving poor, given regular money by the parish
Idle (undeserving) poor, punished and forced to work
Gentry, invited to serve at court
Recusant, fined for his religion
questions.explain: Able-bodied 'idle poor' were treated as vagrants who could be whipped and set to work, unlike the 'deserving poor' who received relief.

questions.q: An MP in the 1570s repeatedly demands the right to debate the queen's marriage and succession freely in Parliament and is imprisoned for it. This best illustrates which feature of Elizabethan government?
options: Elizabeth's willingness to share power fully with Parliament
Tension over parliamentary free speech, which Elizabeth regarded as her royal prerogative
Parliament's firm control over England's foreign policy
The abolition of the monarch's special privileges
questions.explain: Elizabeth insisted matters like marriage, succession and religion were royal prerogatives, clashing with outspoken MPs such as Peter Wentworth.

specSource: AQA GCSE History (8145) specification; Elizabethan England, c1568-1603
